Twenty-six comments

Bill the Weaver’s?

The liner notes on Whistle Stop say that Din Tarrant’s and Bill the Weaver’s are the same tune, but this is the one Brian Hughes plays, not the other entry for Bill the Weaver’s.

As far as I know, Din Tarrant’s is usually played with the A and B parts switched. I entered it the way I heard it on Whistle Stop, though, because I think it sounds better.

↳ Posted by whyfish on July 15th, 2003.

I don’t know the name of this tune, but I think it may be the coolest polka ever.

Locha Cross

I’m sure I have several recordings of this tune. Only one I’ve found so far is by Kerry box-player Denis Doody. He called it “Locha Cross”.
“Patrick Street” have a set of 3 polkas on their 3rd LP starting with “Walsh’s”, but this tune is not one of them. Is there a “Walsh’s” set on one of the other albums?

N: notes by Jackie Small from this lovely CD: “~ Julia Clifford was the source for the intricate polka ‘Bill the Weaver’s’. The title refers to Julia’s father who played the concert flute. Taylor.”

Re: Din Tarrant’s

I went to Gaelic Roots to hear the Sunday night concert, at Boston College 1997
https://www.discogs.com/Various-Boston-College-Irish-Studies-Program-Celebrates-Gaelic-Roots/release/3079897
And Johnny O’Leary played this Din Tarrant’s Polka along with another one which I still don’t know the name. The tunes are listed as the Lonesome Polkas on the Gaelic Roots Cd for that year.

I just played an album on WOMR this past Monday the 23rd 2020 and finally had a name for
1st of Lonesome Polkas. The album was Mighty Session! Kells Music 1997
Track #4

https://thesession.org/recordings/4061

↳ Posted by jamfiddler on November 28th, 2020.

Din Tarrant’s, X:7

An A ‘dorian/minor’ version of this tune transcribed from Kerry Music By Denis Doody

https://thesession.org/recordings/1309

There are no F’s so I believe that qualifies it as hexatonic whence the awesome bluesy-ness (as well as that c# blue note). I have put it as A dorian, because I think it feels more like it would be f#s if they were there.

The recording in general is pitched in a way that you could possible argue he was playing this in B, but having checked with the other tunes on the album, it seems the recording needs increasing by roughly 0.5 to get it to standard pitch. The recording comments has a further explanation as to why this is.
